{{Short description|none}}
The following is a '''list of Laplace transforms''' for many common functions of a single variable.<ref>{{Citation |first1=J. J. |last1=Distefano |first2=A. R. |last2=Stubberud |first3=I. J. |last3=Williams |page=78 |title=Feedback systems and control |edition=2nd |publisher=McGraw-Hill |series=Schaum's outlines |year=1995 |isbn=978-0-07-017052-0}}</ref> The [[Laplace transform]] is an [[integral transform]] that takes a function of a positive real variable {{math|''t''}} (often time) to a function of a complex variable {{mvar|s}} (complex [[angular frequency]]).

==Properties==
{{Main|Laplace transform#Properties and theorems}}

The Laplace transform of a function <math>f(t)</math> can be obtained using the [[Laplace transform#Formal definition|formal definition]] of the Laplace transform. However, some properties of the Laplace transform can be used to obtain the Laplace transform of some functions more easily.

===Linearity===

For functions <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> and for scalar <math>a</math>, the Laplace transform satisfies

: <math>\mathcal{L}\{a f(t) + b g(t)\}  = a \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} + b \mathcal{L}\{ g(t)\}  </math>

and is, therefore, regarded as a linear operator.

===Time shifting===

The Laplace transform of <math> f(t - a) u(t - a) </math>, where <math> u </math> is the Heaviside step function, is <math> e^{-as} F(s) </math>.

===Frequency shifting===

The Laplace transform of <math> e^{at} f(t)  </math> is <math> F(s - a) </math>.

==Explanatory notes==

The unilateral Laplace transform takes as input a function whose time domain is the [[non-negative]] reals, which is why all of the time domain functions in the table below are multiples of the [[Heaviside step function]], {{math|''u''(''t'')}}.

The entries of the table that involve a time delay {{math|''τ''}} are required to be [[causal system|causal]] (meaning that {{math|''τ'' > 0}}).  A causal system is a system where the [[impulse response]] {{math|''h''(''t'')}} is zero for all time {{mvar|t}} prior to {{math|1=''t'' = 0}}. In general, the region of convergence for causal systems is not the same as that of [[anticausal system]]s.

The following functions and variables are used in the table below:

* {{math|''δ''}}  represents the [[Dirac delta function]].
* {{math|''u''(''t'')}} represents the [[Heaviside step function]]. Literature may refer to this by other notation, including <math>1(t)</math> or <math>H(t)</math>.
* {{math|Γ(''z'')}} represents the [[Gamma function]].
* {{math|''γ''}} is the [[Euler&ndash;Mascheroni constant]].
* {{math|''t''}} is a [[real number]]. It typically represents ''time'', although it can represent ''any'' independent dimension.
* {{math|''s''}} is the [[complex number|complex]] frequency domain parameter, and  {{math|Re(''s'')}} is its [[real part]].
* {{math|''n''}} is an [[integer]].
* {{math|''α'', ''τ,'' and ''ω''}} are real numbers.
* {{math|''q''}} is a complex number.
